lines.text: Do you know how solar panels work? They turn sunlight into electricity, with no moving parts at all.
A panel is made of dozens of cells: thin slices of silicon, the same element inside computer chips.
Each cell has two layers. One is treated to have extra electrons, the other to have gaps where electrons are missing. Where they meet, an electric field forms.
When sunlight hits, a photon knocks an electron loose. The field pushes it one way, and the only way back is through a wire.
Billions of electrons flowing through that wire make an electric current. Each cell gives about half a volt, so the cells are wired together.
That's direct current. An inverter flips it into the alternating current your home uses.
Today's panels turn about twenty percent of the sunlight into electricity. Most of the rest becomes heat.
And the sunlight reaching Earth in just one hour carries roughly as much energy as humanity uses in a whole year.
So a solar panel is sunlight, setting electrons in motion.
